steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Draft the introduction for our paper on students' perceptions of fairness, accountability, transparency and ethics (FATE) in multimodal learning analytics, studied in a real classroom deployment. Explain what MMLA is, its challenges, why FATE matters, and state our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. What MMLA is and what it offers
2. Challenges and concerns in MMLA
3. Gap: FATE in authentic deployments
4. Why researching FATE matters
5. This paper and its contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. MMLA
- relatively novel approach in learning analytics (LA); diverse data collection methods to examine complex learning processes
- beyond clickstreams and keystrokes: gestures, body movements, eye movements, facial expressions, hand motions, voice, physiological responses
- multifaceted student interactions -> personalised, adaptive learning environments
- educators/researchers: systems for individual student needs, considering factors that influence learning

2. Challenges
- concerns about technologies used + unforeseen practices
- multi-channel modelling: mapping diverse data to educational constructs
- logistics: complex technical infrastructure -> scalability
- systematic reviews: socio-technical and ethical challenges moving from research settings to classrooms
- advanced sensors in learning spaces may threaten student privacy
- more modalities refine modelling, but no guarantee of fairer results

3. Gap
- research in authentic classrooms scarce: how to use MMLA effectively while addressing FATE concerns emerging in Artificial Intelligence (AI)
- highlighted in MMLA literature, but authentic deployments have not examined FATE thoroughly

4. Why FATE
- vital in LA and MMLA: equitable, responsible, trustworthy systems; benefit broad spectrum of students; no reinforcing biases / accentuating discrimination
- identify boundaries of MMLA in authentic learning setting
- students' perceptions -> inform design of analytics technologies + strategies for ethical use; address threats to acceptance and adoption

5. Contributions
- explore FATE issues in authentic large-scale MMLA deployment
- 1) first evaluation of students' perceptions of FATE in authentic MMLA deployment
- 2) set of specific FATE issues to address in future MMLA studies
- why: fair and accurate representation of learner data; learners' autonomy over personal data; understanding of data collection/analysis; integrity of measurable informed consent

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) is still a fairly new approach in learning analytics (LA). It focuses on collecting data in diverse ways to look at complex learning processes. Instead of only using clickstreams and keystrokes, MMLA also includes other modalities, like gestures, body movements, eye movements, facial expressions, hand motions, voice and physiological responses. Because student interactions have many sides, MMLA can give insights for making learning environments that are personalised and adaptive. With diverse data, educators and researchers can design systems that address the needs of individual students and also consider different factors that influence learning.

MMLA is promising, but there are concerns about the technologies that are used and about practices that nobody foresaw that may come up. One challenge is how complicated multi-channel modelling is, for example mapping diverse data to educational constructs, and there are also logistical issues like complex technical infrastructure, which affects how scalable MMLA is. Systematic reviews keep pointing out socio-technical and ethical challenges when MMLA moves from research settings into classrooms. In particular, using advanced sensors in learning spaces may be a threat to student privacy. More data modalities can refine modelling, but that does not guarantee that the analytical results are fairer. Also, there is not much research in authentic classrooms, so there is a gap in understanding how to use MMLA effectively while also addressing the fairness, accountability, transparency and ethics (FATE) concerns that are emerging in Artificial Intelligence (AI). These issues have been highlighted in the MMLA literature, but authentic MMLA deployments have not looked at them thoroughly yet.

4. Why FATE
- vital in LA and MMLA: equitable, responsible, trustworthy systems; benefit broad spectrum of students; no reinforcing biases / accentuating discrimination
- identify boundaries of MMLA in authentic learning setting
- students' perceptions -> inform design of analytics technologies + strategies for ethical use; address threats to acceptance and adoption

5. Contributions
- explore FATE issues in authentic large-scale MMLA deployment
- 1) first evaluation of students' perceptions of FATE in authentic MMLA deployment
- 2) set of specific FATE issues to address in future MMLA studies
- why: fair and accurate representation of learner data; learners' autonomy over personal data; understanding of data collection/analysis; integrity of measurable informed consent

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) is still a fairly new approach in learning analytics (LA). It focuses on collecting data in diverse ways to look at complex learning processes. Instead of only using clickstreams and keystrokes, MMLA also includes other modalities, like gestures, body movements, eye movements, facial expressions, hand motions, voice and physiological responses. Because student interactions have many sides, MMLA can give insights for making learning environments that are personalised and adaptive. With diverse data, educators and researchers can design systems that address the needs of individual students and also consider different factors that influence learning.

MMLA is promising, but there are concerns about the technologies that are used and about practices that nobody foresaw that may come up. One challenge is how complicated multi-channel modelling is, for example mapping diverse data to educational constructs, and there are also logistical issues like complex technical infrastructure, which affects how scalable MMLA is. Systematic reviews keep pointing out socio-technical and ethical challenges when MMLA moves from research settings into classrooms. In particular, using advanced sensors in learning spaces may be a threat to student privacy. More data modalities can refine modelling, but that does not guarantee that the analytical results are fairer. Also, there is not much research in authentic classrooms, so there is a gap in understanding how to use MMLA effectively while also addressing the fairness, accountability, transparency and ethics (FATE) concerns that are emerging in Artificial Intelligence (AI). These issues have been highlighted in the MMLA literature, but authentic MMLA deployments have not looked at them thoroughly yet.

It is vital to research FATE in LA and MMLA. It can help design LA systems that are equitable, responsible and trustworthy, so that they benefit a broad range of students and do not reinforce existing biases or make discrimination worse. In the same way, studying FATE in MMLA is needed to find the boundaries of MMLA in an authentic learning setting. Previous studies have said that understanding how students perceive FATE issues can help inform the creation of analytics technologies and the strategies around using them ethically, and it can also help address possible threats to acceptance and adoption.

This paper starts to work on this area by exploring FATE issues in an authentic large-scale MMLA deployment. The contribution of this study is two-fold: 1) we present the first evaluation of how students perceive FATE issues in an authentic MMLA deployment, and 2) we identify a set of specific FATE issues that future MMLA studies need to address. Addressing these issues is essential so that MMLA gives a fair and accurate representation of learner data, respects the autonomy of learners over their personal data, helps learners understand the data collection and analysis processes, and keeps the integrity of achieving measurable informed consent.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) is still a relatively novel approach in learning analytics (LA), focusing on diverse data collection methods to examine complex learning processes [1,2]. Rather than using only clickstreams and keystrokes, MMLA includes other modalities such as gestures [3], body movements [4], eye movements [5], facial expressions [6], hand motions [7], voice [8], and physiological responses [9]. By recognising the multifaceted nature of student interactions, MMLA offers insights for creating personalised, adaptive learning environments [10]. Leveraging diverse data, educators and researchers can design systems that address individual student needs while considering the different factors that influence learning [11].

Despite its promise, there are concerns about the technologies used in MMLA and about unforeseen practices that may arise [12,10,2,13]. Challenges include the intricacies of multi-channel modelling, such as mapping diverse data to educational constructs [13,14], as well as logistical issues, like complex technical infrastructure, that impact MMLA scalability [15,16]. Systematic reviews consistently point out socio-technical and ethical challenges when MMLA moves from research settings to classrooms [12,15,17,18]. In particular, the use of advanced sensors in learning spaces may threaten student privacy [12]. While more data modalities can refine modelling [19], they do not guarantee fairer analytical results [20]. Moreover, research in authentic classrooms remains scarce, leaving a gap in understanding how to use MMLA effectively while addressing the emerging fairness, accountability, transparency, and ethics (FATE) concerns in Artificial Intelligence (AI) [21]. Although these issues have been highlighted in the MMLA literature [17,10,2,22], authentic MMLA deployments have yet to examine them thoroughly.

Researching FATE in LA and MMLA is vital [21,23]. It can foster the design of LA systems that are equitable, responsible, and trustworthy, ensuring that they benefit a broad spectrum of students without reinforcing existing biases or accentuating discrimination [23]. Likewise, studying FATE in MMLA is essential for identifying the boundaries of MMLA in an authentic learning setting [12]. Previous studies have emphasised that understanding students’ perceptions of FATE issues can help inform the creation of analytics technologies and the strategies for their ethical use [24,21], as well as address potential threats to acceptance and adoption [25]. This paper makes inroads into this area by exploring FATE issues in the context of an authentic large-scale MMLA deployment. The contribution of this study is two-fold: 1) we present the first evaluation of students’ perceptions of FATE issues in an authentic MMLA deployment, and 2) we identify a set of specific FATE issues that need to be addressed in future MMLA studies. Addressing these issues is essential to ensure that MMLA provides a fair and accurate representation of learner data, respects learners’ autonomy over their personal data, fosters learners’ understanding of data collection and analysis processes, and upholds the integrity of achieving measurable informed consent.
